articles.title: Caitlin Clark and the Fever have championship potential, but what-ifs and uncertainty reign after latest ousting by Aces
articles.summary: “Obviously we live in a world of instant gratification, and everybody expects me to win a championship immediately,” Caitlin Clark said.
articles.body:
LAS VEGAS — Caitlin Clark touched her tooth, a reflexive move she added to her repertoire within the last hour or so at Michelob Ultra Arena. The ask of her to think back about what stands out about her third professional season is a big one. She mentions "tremendous" teammates, including her podium-mate Kelsey Mitchell, as having the best season of any guard that's ever been in the WNBA. She notes the close-knit locker room. That she's overall proud.

"There's obviously so much outside noise on a microscope of how we perform every single day," Clark said on the final day of her season, a 94-83 Game 3 loss to the Las Vegas Aces in the first round of the WNBA playoffs barely in the rearview. "A lot of really good moments. A lot of tough moments, too, where we felt like we gave a lot of opportunities away, and it's probably what hurts a little bit."

The Fever began the season with championship aspirations that could have been realized. The team set offensive records in the league's 30th season. Clark and Mitchell finished second and third, respectively, in average scoring behind presumptive fifth-time MVP A'ja Wilson. In a stressful return from soft tissue injuries that limited her to 13 games last year, Clark finished second in assists.

The Fever were at times the best in the league, a team you couldn't count out even if they were down by 20. Other times, it felt as though they couldn't dig out of the mud if it were mostly water. They were too much of a roller coaster ride to trust. Out of the FIFA World Cup break, they took a sharp downward swing from a top-four seed to No. 6 of eight.

But! But! The No. 3 Aces are an advantageous matchup, came the cries of fans holding onto desperate hope. This was meant to be . And honestly, it lined up. Indiana went 2-1 against them in the regular season. The Aces' defense was faulty. Their offense relied too heavily on Wilson, and Aliyah Boston could limit her like few others.

Everyone missed the forest for the trees. And not the ones hounding Mitchell all week in the paint.

The same issues that plagued the Fever in Clark's rookie year remain. Clark mentioned several times on Thursday that it was only her fifth playoff game. By midnight on the East Coast, that number hit six. Two days prior, she earned her first professional postseason win in takeover fashion . Those numbers aren't all that different for Mitchell or Boston, though each played in eight playoff games last year while Clark watched from the bench.

The experience meter hasn't budged all that much from 2024 , when the Fever reached the playoffs for the first time since Tamika Catchings retired in 2016. In Clark, Boston and even veteran Mitchell's first playoffs, a graphic hammered home the larger point. The Fever's 11 players had 19 games of postseason experience collectively. Their first-round opponent that year, a Connecticut Sun squad led by now-Fever head coach Stephanie White, had nearly 12 times as many at 222.

The team at the top was — and remains, two years later — Las Vegas. The 2024 roster combined for 273 games of experience. The core players that have remained have each added 16 more games since then, plus two championships. The Fever still aren't anywhere close, and arguably, few others are, either.

"As a group, we're still getting our feet wet on the playoff experience side and we played against a team that's full of playoff experience," Mitchell said. "So that speaks for itself."

For the second consecutive season, the Aces ended the Fever's postseason and will play in their eighth straight semifinals. Vegas' big three, as always, turned up the way Hammon always expects. Wilson (36 points), Chelsea Gray (23 points) and Jackie Young (18) combined for 77 of the Aces' 94.

For the last four years, the Aces ended quite nearly everyone's season. The only series they've lost is the 2024 semifinals to the New York Liberty, a "superteam" roster that added two veteran MVPs to compete with the reigning champion Aces.

Las Vegas is homegrown, a squad that built through the collegiate draft in the late 2010s and is reaping the rewards of lucky lottery balls. The franchise drafted Kelsey Plum, the former all-time NCAA women's Division I scorer, first overall in their final year as the San Antonio Stars in 2017. A'ja Wilson, an NCAA champion at South Carolina, came in at No. 1 in 2018. Jackie Young joined as the No. 1 pick out of Notre Dame in 2019, a season removed from her own NCAA title.

The Fever drafted Boston, a South Carolina champion, and Clark, the active NCAA women's and men's all-time leading scorer, in 2023 and 2024, respectively. It takes a blind eye — or potentially one on the other side of a budding and tense rivalry — to not see the parallels between the two.

"No," Hammon said when asked if she sees the likeness, but noted the team has potential. On a follow-up: "I see differences. And I'll keep those to myself."

There is minutiae in the comparison. And though Hammon wouldn't divulge, there are differentiators. Each team with back-to-back No. 1 picks has won within three years together, but it's more like year 2 for Clark and Co. It's also a different league than when the Aces stacked selections, and certainly from when the Seattle Storm had consecutive top picks in 2001-02 and 2015-16.

"Obviously we live in a world of instant gratification, and everybody expects me to win a championship immediately," Clark said. "And certainly that's my goal. I think this team has potential to do that."

Potential. It's the same word Hammon used. In the future, in a slightly different way, facing a team not actively writing a dynasty.

The Aces endured their own heartbreak en route to a title. They lost the 2020 WNBA Finals, a series that Wilson has used as fuel. Team owner Mark Davis built them the league's first standalone practice facility specifically for their use. After a semifinal berth in 2021, they signed Hammon to what was then the largest coaching contract in the league. She's ended the season with a parade in three of four tries, and is attempting to make it a fourth.

And yet, the Fever were right there with the league standard bearers again, despite earning a 'C' on Clark's report card. Following a messy blowout, they defended home court with an offensive masterclass that involved each of the big three in Game 2 .

The winner-take-all matchup in an uninviting Michelob Ultra Arena went down to the wire after the Fever trailed by as many as 12 in a chippy, foul-filled affair. They were 14 of 20 from the line, paling in comparison to the Aces' 28 of 35. The numbers were starker in the first half. Double technicals were assessed to Clark and Brianna Turner. White looked apoplectic at a call made on Lexie Hull defending Wilson, and was unable to use a challenge. She, too, earned a tech.

Of many pivotal plays in hindsight, one stood clear in the moment. After Mitchell's stepback 3 pulled the Fever to within a possession, 82-80, Clark stole the ball from Gray. Mitchell missed a floater, but the bouncy vet leaped up for the rebound. She snaggled with Gray under the basket and was called for the foul. White challenged, using her final timeout, and the call stood. Gray made both free throws.

"Things didn't go our way tonight, but if the challenge at whatever point that was, two minutes to go, is called correctly when they go to the monitor, it's a one-possession game and we have the ball," Clark said.

It swung the game, but it did not define it. The Fever's offense — which Hammon praised as "impressive" — never hit full strength after a 31-31 first quarter. They were 38.5% from the floor, third-worst of their season. They lost all eight games in which they were worse than 42%. Their perimeter shooting (9 of 32) let them down, and late, momentum-shifting attempts by Mitchell and Clark both bounced.

"We've made a lot of those shots throughout the year, too," Clark said. "So if we would have ran it back, who knows, me and Kels maybe make another combined eight shots, and it's a completely different game."

Like much of the season, the opportunity slipped away. The Fever walked off the court for the last time this year, and with a finality to this version of themselves. They've gained experience. The front office will adjust out of necessity. Mitchell, most notably, is a free agent and will be highly sought after should she want to take the calls. She's only ever played in Indiana after being drafted No. 2 after Wilson. The salary cap will dictate options.

In a different version of these playoffs, which Clark assessed as wide open, the Fever advance and lend credence to their preseason claims. Yet, they dealt themselves their own hand and didn't have the cards to beat the best.

articles.title: La indultada A'ja Wilson se carga a Caitlin Clark en la WNBA
articles.standfirst: A'ja Wilson vuelve a brillar ante Indiana y planta a Las Vegas en semifinales de la WNBA
articles.summary: A'ja Wilson vuelve a brillar ante Indiana y planta a Las Vegas en semifinales de la WNBA
articles.body: Las Aces de Las Vegas se plantaron nuevamente en semifinales de la WNBA con una victoria (94-83) en el tercer partido frente a las India Fever de Caitlin Clark. Volvió a brillar su pivot estrella A'ja Wilson, que no fue suspendida tras encararse con un aficionado, que anotó 34 puntos y sumó 9 rebotes. El duelo a todo o nada con dos de las mejores de la WNBA sobre la cancha, Wilson y Caitlin Clark, no decepcionó de inicio, incluso cuando las Aces tuvieran que salir sin Stephanie Talbot, la encargada de defender hasta ahora a la base de Indiana en la serie, descartada por lesión de última hora. Con Indiana mejor de inicio y una Clark casi impecable desde la línea de 3, Las Vegas respondió cerrando el primer cuarto con un parcial de 8-2 que dejó el marcador en tablas (31-31), y Wilson anotando 14 puntos y logrando un 100 % en tiros de campo. Las vigentes campeonas, y ganadoras en tres de las últimas cuatro temporadas, mantuvieron el ritmo mientras las del Medio Oeste comenzaron a mostrarse menos efectivas en ataque (acumularon casi cuatro minutos sin mover su casillero) hacia el final del segundo cuarto, lo que dejó a Las Vegas con una ventaja de seis con la mitad del partido por disputar. Wilson siguió a lo suyo, con la cuatro veces MVP siendo un martillo en ataque, mientras Clark se desdibujó durante varios minutos, dejando de intentar el tiro mientras su equipo seguía fallando demasiado desde la pintura. Las Aces llegaron a mandar de 12, pero llegaron al último cuarto solo con una ventaja de 5 puntos gracias a un parcial de 9-3 para las de Indiana, que, en todo caso, tampoco conseguían alcanzar los porcentajes de triples que han mostrado esta temporada. Fever logró ponerse a solo 2 gracias a un muy buen arranque en el último tramo de 10 minutos, pero las campeonas mantuvieron el tipo y lograban mantener a Indiana a distancia prudencial. Fue entonces cuando, a poco más de 3 minutos del final y con Las Vegas liderando 82-77, Clark se llevó un codazo de Jewell Lloyd en un rebote defensivo que le abrió el encía y obligó a parar el partido un par de minutos. La base de Iowa logró retornar y Kelsey Mitchell apareció por fin para anotar un triple que volvía a poner a su equipo a solo dos puntos. Pero la propia Mitchell volvió a desenfocarse cuando más se la necesitaba, dejando escapar fuera bajo el aro un pase interior, una jugada que escenificó el pésimo fin de partido en ataque de Indiana, que acabaría 11 por debajo (94-83) cuando sonó el silbato final. Las Aces se enfrentarán en semifinales, a partir del 4 de octubre, al equipo que gane el definitivo tercer partido entre las Valkyries y las Wings en San Francisco.

articles.title: Jalen Duren traga con 200 millones y su aversión a la báscula: el pívot All-Star sigue en los Pistons
articles.standfirst: Jalen Duren, que optaba a un máximo de 287 millones por cinco años, acepta los 200 millones por 5 años que le ofrecieron los Pistons y que dos semanas atrás rechazo
articles.summary: Jalen Duren, que optaba a un máximo de 287 millones por cinco años, acepta los 200 millones por 5 años que le ofrecieron los Pistons y que dos semanas atrás rechazo
articles.body: Jalen Duren acordó un contrato de cinco años y 200 millones de dólares totalmente garantizados para regresar a los Detroit Pistons, según adelantó su agente Chafie Fields a Shams Charania de la cadena ESPN. El joven jugador de 22 años, que no se presentó a la pretemporada ni el Media Day de los Pistons, zanjó de esta manera una disputa salarial que se ha alargado durante cuatro meses y en la que optaba a un contrato multianual máximo de 287 millones por cinco años. Duren, que era agente libre restringido y fue All Star en 2026, había rechazado dos semanas atrás esa oferta del equipo por 5 años y 200 millones. Si no hubiese aceptado la propuesta de tendría que haberse conformado con una oferta cualificada de 1 año y 9,6 millones, que lo habría convertido en agente libre sin restricciones el próximo verano. Fuentes informaron a Charania a principios de esta semana que sus representantes dejaron claro que el jugador se sentía menospreciado por el proceso, especialmente en comparación con la gestión del equipo respecto a la extensión de contrato del alero Ausar Thompson, quien acordó a principios de mes un contrato de cinco años y 155 millones de dólares bajo la escala salarial para novatos. Duren, que la pasada temporada promedió 19,5 puntos y 10,5 rebotes con un 65 % de acierto en el tiro, también mostró su desacuerdo con las cláusulas relativas al peso incluidas en algunas de las ofertas anteriores del equipo.

articles.title: Zaragoza confirma la marcha en diciembre de Mariona Ortiz a la Project B de Djokovic y Westbrook
articles.standfirst: "Mariona Ortiz ha comunicado al club su decisión de resolver anticipadamente su contrato para incorporarse a un nuevo proyecto global de baloncesto"
articles.summary: "Mariona Ortiz ha comunicado al club su decisión de resolver anticipadamente su contrato para incorporarse a un nuevo proyecto global de baloncesto"
articles.body: La capitana del Casademont Zaragoza, Mariona Ortiz, se desvinculará del club el 30 de diciembre de 2026, pero, hasta entonces, seguirá "formando parte del equipo y compitiendo" a las órdenes de Carlos Cantero, según informó este viernes la entidad. "Mariona Ortiz ha comunicado al club su decisión de resolver anticipadamente su contrato para incorporarse a un nuevo proyecto global de baloncesto", reza la nota del equipo aragonés. Ese nuevo reto para Ortiz es 'Project B', una nueva liga que comenzará en enero de 2027, que está reclutando a algunas de las mejores jugadoras del mundo con sueldos millonarios y se solapará con la competición europea. Mariona Ortiz, integrante de la selección española que obtuvo la medalla de bronce en el reciente Mundial de Berlín, se convierte así en la segunda baloncestista española tras Awa Fam que deja la Liga Femenina Endesa para fichar por 'Project B'. Detrás de este nuevo proyecto están inversores de conocidas compañías además de deportistas como Novak Djokovic o Russell Westbrook. A un día de que comience la nueva temporada de liga, la noticia ha sido un golpe duro para la 'Marea Roja', que ve como su máxima referente no terminará la temporada con el club al que llegó hace cinco temporadas. Cabe recordar que en 2027, el Príncipe Felipe será sede de la Copa de la Reina y de la Final a Seis de la Euroliga. Por su parte, la base catalana, líder indiscutible del Zaragoza desde su llegada, ha querido trasladar un mensaje a la afición y al club: "Siento de todo corazón la forma en la que os habéis enterado. No era la que estaba planeada, ni la que me hubiera gustado, y mucho menos, la que os merecéis". Además, la internacional explicó que lo dará "todo por y para este club" hasta que finalice su compromiso el 30 de diciembre

articles.title: NBA closes sole Africa training academy in blow to young players
articles.summary: NBA says its focus is on new global academy opening in Abu Dhabi as Africa, Mexico and Australia hit by closures.
articles.body:
The NBA has closed its only elite training academy in Africa, less than a decade after it was launched in Senegal to prepare promising young African players for professional leagues in the United States and elsewhere.

The decision to close NBA Academy Africa was a blow to students and young players across the continent, two former employees said.

Michel Chikwanine, who had been the academy’s performance and lifestyle adviser, said late on Thursday that the news discouraged African players just beginning to build confidence.

“From the moment we told them, their confidence waned, their confidence dropped,” he said.

Michael Abbott, former head of academic planning at the academy, said it showed a lack of commitment to the students.

“They weren’t invested in them as kids as much as they were invested in the business model,” he said.

In response to questions from the Reuters news agency, the NBA said the decision reflected a shift in global basketball development strategy. It has previously closed academies in Mexico and Australia. All training will be run out of a new global academy to open soon in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates, it said.

In its statement, the NBA added that it is continuing to invest in African talent through other programmes and closing the academy does not signal a diminished commitment to the continent.

It cited examples such as the creation of a Basketball Africa League, which has concluded six seasons, and Basketball Without Borders, which organises elite training camps for young people worldwide, including in Africa.

NBA success in Africa followed by closure

NBA Academy Africa has trained about 110 students since launching in Senegal in 2018, Abbott said, and many have moved on to elite schools and universities in the US. The most successful students were drafted into the NBA.

Graduate Ulrich Kamka Chomche of Cameroon became the first player to be drafted into the NBA in 2024 and played for the Toronto Raptors. Former academy student Khaman Maluach of South Sudan plays for the Phoenix Suns.

Chikwanine said closing the academy will limit opportunities for African players, who often come from challenging backgrounds and need specific support. All African prospects will have to compete globally for spots in the UAE.

He said the NBA’s decision reinforced a message felt by many Africans that big companies come to the continent claiming to want to invest in people but in reality just want to make money.

“They come in with an extraction mindset,” he said. “That has always been a reality on the continent of Africa. … There is a huge mistrust that has been built.”

The NBA denied that closing the academy would limit opportunities for young African players. It said training all young players at a single location would give them greater exposure to professional coaches and scouts worldwide.

“We’re incredibly proud of the impact that NBA Academy Africa has had and remain committed to developing the next generation of African players,” Troy Justice, NBA senior vice president, said in a statement, adding that several other youth development initiatives still operate on the continent.

articles.title: NBA Power Rankings Entering 2026 Preseason
articles.summary: After a wild NBA offseason and with media days in the books, it's time to break down the league in another edition of the power rankings.
articles.body:
After a wild NBA offseason and with media days in the books, it's time to break down the league in another edition of the power rankings.

Almost every organization is brimming with hope right now, but it's more warranted in some cases than others. Wherever your team falls on that line, you'll find it ranked by the criteria that have guided us for years.

Based on team and player stats, recent performance (in this week's case, last season), championship chances and plenty of subjectivity, here's where all 30 teams stand as training camps open across the NBA.

ATL | BKN | BOS | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

After the league handed down its punishment for the Los Angeles Clippers' cap circumvention and the Kawhi Leonard trade finally and officially went through, this team was always going to have a rough 2026-27.

On media day, the outlook somehow got even bleaker when it was revealed that Brandon Ingram would miss the start of the regular season after the medical staff discovered a partially torn Achilles.

There are still some veteran contributors left (like Darius Garland and Brook Lopez). Keaton Wagler is a source of hope in a tough organizational moment. But things are going to look and feel very rough in the wake of a Kawhi era that yielded little more than penalties.

Ben Simmons was the big story for the Sacramento Kings in the media, which is a pretty rough indicator of how the season will go.

The three-time All-Star missed all of last season. In the last three campaigns he did play, he averaged 5.9 points and shot 52.4 percent from the free-throw line.

When the novelty of his comeback wears off, the attention will quickly shift back to who, if anyone, will give the Kings a shred of value for Domantas Sabonis and Zach LaVine.

The Milwaukee Bucks should be, at the very least, scrappy. In what Adam Silver is surely hoping is a post-tanking world, scrappy may not be good enough to avoid the bottom of the standings.

Still, even in this first year without Giannis Antetokounmpo, Bucks fans have reason to be optimistic.

When Ryan Rollins, Tyler Herro and Jaime Jaquez are on the floor, Milwaukee should be competitive. No one in that trio is old, though they're far from the biggest sources of upside.

That's Brayden Burries, who has the potential to be one of the best playmakers from his draft class.

Ranking Every NBA Team's Starting Lineup Ahead of Preseason 🔢

Depth will be a pretty significant problem for the Brooklyn Nets. However, after acquiring Julius Randle, the starting five should have enough firepower to at least make life difficult for opponents.

He and Michael Porter Jr. have produced 20-point-per-game seasons. At least in theory, Randle's slashing should pair well with MPJ's outside shooting.

The real pivot point for this team may be the development of 6'8" playmaker Egor Dëmin, who averaged 11.9 points and 3.2 assists in 26.9 minutes, while shooting 40.6 percent from deep, over his last 30 games as a rookie.

If the 20-year-old takes a couple of natural steps forward, Brooklyn might even threaten for a play-in spot.

After several years hovering somewhere between hopeless and mediocre, the Chicago Bulls are finally giving their fans something to look forward to with the forward duo of Matas Buzelis and rookie Caleb Wilson.

Both have multi-positional versatility. Both have great size. Both are good (and in Wilson's case, great) athletes. Wilson, at least, has superstar upside.

Surrounding those two with Josh Giddey's playmaking and veteran acquisitions like Norman Powell and Nicolas Claxton should expedite their development.

Though they're not a safe bet to make the playoffs, the Bulls at least appear to be headed in that direction over the next few years.

The Memphis Grizzlies are going to be one of those young teams that don't know better than to play with maximum effort every night. They'll annoy the heck out of regular-season coasters and likely improve on last season's win total.

Cameron Boozer has the most upside of anyone behind that formula, but there's reason for optimism with Cedric Coward, Zach Edey and Jaylen Wells too.

Supplementing them with veterans like Ty Jerome, Isaiah Stewart and Jerami Grant could make the Grizzlies a surprise play-in contender.

For years, the New Orleans Pelicans have struggled to live up to the talent on their roster.

For this one, like others before it, it's hard to look at names like Zion Williamson, Trey Murphy III and Dejounte Murray and not think they have a chance to be one of this season's surprise teams.

But lack of shooting from regulars other than Murphy and lack of durability from Zion (though he did manage 62 appearances last season) will likely doom them to the lottery again.

Stephen Curry gave us one of media day's most viral moments with his reaction above to the idea of missing the playoffs.

Maybe he shouldn't be all that surprised by the notion. Golden State has finished in the lottery four of the last seven seasons. Moses Moody is likely to miss the whole season. Jimmy Butler could miss most of it. On Monday, we learned that Kristaps Porziņģis is once again out with an undisclosed medical issue.

Curry took a lot of pressure off the front office by signing another contract extension, but that didn't take much off him. It's going to take a truly Herculean effort for the 38-year-old guard to carry the Warriors through all of the above.

After trading for Jaren Jackson Jr. in February and landing Darryn Peterson in the draft, the Utah Jazz look poised to turn the corner from rebuild to competitiveness.

Pairing those two with Lauri Markkanen, Keyonte George and (likely) Jusuf Nurkić will make for a big, explosive starting five. If they take a few more developmental steps forward, Isaiah Collier and Ace Bailey could lead a dynamic bench.

The West is crowded, as always, but the Jazz have enough talent to push for a playoff spot.

After being perhaps the biggest surprise team of the 2025-26 season, the Phoenix Suns traded away depth and shooting from Royce O'Neale and Grayson Allen for a bigger-upside swing in Miles Bridges.

The move was also a bet that Devin Booker and Dillon Brooks could maintain the culture and identity that made them so much better than expected last season.

If they come through on that bet and a couple of the younger players (like Khaman Maluach or Koa Peat) pop, Phoenix could take another step in the right direction this season.

In 2024-25, the Detroit Pistons became the first team in NBA history to triple their win total from the previous campaign. Just a couple of years later, the Washington Wizards have a chance to do the same.

Now, that's only possible because of how dreadful Washington was last season. Getting to 51 wins would be a s tretch (their over/under is set at 33.5).

Assuming they stay healthy, Trae Young and Anthony Davis could be one of the most explosive guard-big duos in the league. Top overall pick AJ Dybantsa looks ready to contribute right away.

If one or two of the holdovers from the young core take steps forward, another historic improvement could be on the way.

With Kyrie Irving coming back, Cooper Flagg looking at a second-year leap and Dusty May in place to put all the pieces together between them, it's tempting to pick the Dallas Mavericks as a dark horse to make the West's top six.

That'd be a pretty significant leap, but Kyrie averaged 25.9 points and 5.1 assists over his last three seasons. Flagg had LeBron James-like production as a rookie, putting up 21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists.

Sprinkling in some veteran leadership and toughness from P.J. Washington, a course correction for former first overall pick Zaccharie Risacher and maybe one other breakout candidate like Sergio de Larrea could mean a playoff spot is very much in play.

After being one of last season's biggest breakouts, the Portland Trail Blazers were exactly the kind of team that could take a swing on Ja Morant.

It didn't cost them any piece of the young core. With Shaedon Sharpe hurt, Portland could actually use some of the scoring that a healthy Morant might provide.

The team is still very much Deni Avdija's, but supplementing last season's backcourt with Morant and a post-prime (and post-Achilles tear) Damian Lillard raises its ceiling.

The Charlotte Hornets made one of the boldest bets of the offseason by trading their lead playmaker and face of the franchise, LaMelo Ball. They will be trusting Kon Knueppel, Brandon Miller and Coby White to pick up the slack.

The early returns hit a snag because of Knueppel's offseason hamstring injury, but once he's healthy, it's not hard to imagine this quickly becoming one of the league's most explosive offenses.

He, Miller and White are all dynamic three-point shooters. Now, adding Allen, O'Neale, and Naz Reid gives the Hornets a shot at breaking the single-season record for made threes.

Thanks to the risky trade that landed them Ivica Zubac, the Indiana Pacers' Tyrese Haliburton-less gap year didn't yield a lottery pick.

But at this point in their careers, the bigger and better-rebounding Zubac is likely an upgrade over Myles Turner. That's the only change in a starting lineup that led the Pacers to the NBA Finals.

With Haliburton back, Indiana suddenly has some of the best starters in the East again. TJ McConnell, Kelly Oubre and Obi Toppin provide solid depth.

As Indiana's social media team says above, this team is indeed "so back."

It feels like a borderline make-or-break season for the Orlando Magic, who've failed to live up to expectations in each of the last two seasons after breaking out with 47 wins in 2023-24.

Their two most talented players may be at the core of the disappointment.

Individually, there's plenty to like about both Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner, but their games haven't quite meshed enough for Orlando to be a contender.

In the four years they've been together, the team has performed significantly better when Franz plays without Paolo than it does with any other configuration involving them. If that trend carries into this season, Orlando might have to think about breaking them up.

With Jalen Johnson, Dyson Daniels, Onyeka Okongwu and Nickeil Alexander-Walker, the Atlanta Hawks are absolutely loaded with length, athleticism and defensive tenacity at the top of the roster.

Thanks to the dreaded second apron, the Oklahoma City Thunder salary dumped Luguentz Dort and Aaron Wiggins Atlanta's way, boosting the Hawks' depth and giving them a little championship experience.

There are some pretty serious shooting concerns after Alexander-Walker and CJ McCollum. Okongwu is certainly a bit undersized at the 5. That said, things are clearly heading in the right direction for this team.

Now that most of the player movement and the Clippers investigation are in the rearview, the ongoing stalemate between Jalen Duren and the Detroit Pistons is probably the biggest story in the NBA.

With Duren sitting out media day, the story's only gotten bigger. At this point, it's starting to look like there's a real chance he won't sign a long-term deal in Detroit.

For his part, Cade Cunningham is saying the right things right now, but his job could be harder if Duren isn't around for the 2026-27 campaign (depending on what might come back in a sign-and-trade).

If a deal is aimed more toward the future, the Detroit Pistons would have to slide a little bit in this exercise. If they keep him or move him in a more win-now deal, there could be an argument for moving them up.

At the moment, Duren's indecision makes it tough to pin them down at any spot.

The Los Angeles Lakers said all the right things at media day.

If the players can be trusted, the offense will be more free-flowing. The candidates for the fourth and fifth starting spots (after Luka Dončić, Austin Reaves, and Walker Kessler) will do whatever they're asked. Luka and Reaves will take up LeBron James' leadership mantle without skipping a beat.

But none of that will really matter if L.A. can't cobble together an average or near-average defense. That responsibility will fall largely to coach JJ Redick and Kessler, but previously uncommitted (at least at times) defenders like Luka and Reaves will have to find conviction fast.

If they do, the Lakers have more than enough firepower to be a sneaky title contender. If they don't, they could be fighting for a play-in spot.

The range of outcomes for what is perhaps the league's premier franchise is wide.

After the league's investigation into the Clippers concluded and Kawhi escaped darn-near scot-free (thanks to a deal between the NBA and the players' union), he was all smiles at media day on Monday.

Just like he was in 2018, when he joined the Toronto Raptors the first time around, Kawhi looks like the missing piece to a championship puzzle.

It's hard to overstate the level of upgrade a healthy Leonard is over Ingram. Adding him while still having Scottie Barnes and Collin Murray-Boyles on the roster could give Toronto one of the toughest defenses in the league.

That and Leonard's ability to take over games on the other end make Toronto a bona fide threat to win it all.

The 2025-26 Houston Rockets had one of the league's more embarrassing first-round exits when the Luka-less Lakers sent them packing.

Even with Kevin Durant on the roster and after winning 52 games last season, that version of the team always had plenty of upside for future campaigns.

Reed Sheppard, Alperen Şengün and Jabari Smith Jr. are all still years shy of their primes. Getting Fred VanVleet back from injury will add some stability. KD looks like he could casually drain contested jumpers into his 40s.

But the biggest swing player here is Amen Thompson. Houston is clearly invested in his superstar potential. Beyond signing him to a five-year, $208 million extension, the Rockets hired famed shooting guru Chip Engelland to improve his jumper.

If Thompson adds even an average three-point shot to his defense, playmaking and slashing, he could become a perennial All-NBA player.

Much has been made of the lack of spacing in a Giannis Antetokounmpo-and-Bam Adebayo-led lineup. The concern is fair.

Neither commands a ton of attention beyond the three-point line. Having two such players on the floor can make it hard to play a modern offense.

The front office did a solid job of filling out the rest of the rotation with good-to-great shooters. Last season, Davion Mitchell, Klay Thompson, Andrew Wiggins, Tim Hardaway Jr. and Bobby Portis shot a combined 40.8 percent from deep.

If they stay around that level, while Mitchell, Adebayo and Giannis lead a strong defense, the Heat could be in the mix for a championship.

The Cleveland Cavaliers were flat-out embarrassed by the New York Knicks in the conference finals. They weren't just swept. They lost those four games by an average of 19.3 points.

For some front offices, that would've been enough to warrant a dramatic shakeup. Maybe if things aren't going well in February, that could still happen.

Cleveland opted for continuity and stability instead. James Harden, Donovan Mitchell, Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen are all back. Key reserves like Sam Merrill and Jaylon Tyson are too.

The team didn't stand entirely pat. Adding Peyton Watson's length and athleticism to the mix adds elements on both ends of the floor. If his one-on-one scoring during last season's Nikola Jokić absence is real, the Cavs may suddenly be dynamic enough to avenge last summer's embarrassment.

The loss of Peyton Watson wasn't ideal, but the Denver Nuggets still have one of the NBA's best starting fives.

While Denver has real concerns about its athletic deficit compared to younger teams like the San Antonio Spurs and Oklahoma City Thunder, its starting five and improved bench give the Nuggets a shot.

Assuming it jells, a second unit with Tyus Jones, Julian Strawther, DeMar DeRozan, Spencer Jones and Marvin Bagley can at least match opposing benches. That would be a significant step up from previous years.

Although Rudy Gobert should uphold much of the defense, losing Julius Randle and Naz Reid means the Minnesota Timberwolves will have a slightly different identity than they've had in recent years.

That'll take some getting used to, but the upside is potentially higher with LaMelo Ball around to make life easier for Anthony Edwards.

LaMelo is one of the best playmakers and distributors in the league. He commands far more respect as a three-point shooter than Randle did. He and Ant could be the most explosive backcourt in the NBA.

If Gobert and McDaniels can keep this team in or around the top 10 on defense and Ball can charge the offense a bit, the Timberwolves will stay in the mix for a championship.

Now that the dust has settled on the Jaylen Brown trade, people should be able to look at the 2026-27 Boston Celtics a little more objectively.

They won 56 games last season, missing Jayson Tatum for most of it. He's now in Brown's place. Paul George is theoretically filling Tatum's old roster spot, which didn't give Boston anything till the spring.

Tatum and George are surrounded by the same supporting cast (plus Mitchell Robinson) and infrastructure as last season. That means Boston is still a legitimate contender in the Eastern Conference.

Availability is a concern for Joel Embiid and LeBron James. It'll take some time to figure out the scoring balance between them, Jaylen Brown and Tyrese Maxey. Even second-year guard VJ Edgecombe is in for a pretty big adjustment.

But there is a ton of raw talent here that goes beyond the loaded starting five. A second unit with Anfernee Simons, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Dean Wade will get plenty of minutes.

Assuming everyone is relatively healthy in the spring and summer, Philadelphia will be one of the deeper teams in the East, as they will have a real shot at the championship

The lack of a contract extension for Karl-Anthony Towns could create some awkwardness. Losing Mitchell Robinson this offseason could prove to be a big problem.

Things aren't perfect for New York, but in the short term, the issues feel like nits that might not even need picking.

The championship-winning starting five is back. It has championship experience now. Jalen Brunson's ascension to superstardom doesn't feel over.

No one has repeated as NBA champions since 2018, but Brunson, Towns, OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges and Josh Hart will give this team a chance.

The Oklahoma City Thunder cut into their depth in an effort to stay under the second apron for 2026-27.

Aaron Wiggins, Isaiah Joe and Luguentz Dort are all gone, which could put a real dent in OKC's title prospects.

A healthier Jalen Williams and meaningful steps forward for young players like Nikola Topić, Thomas Sorber and Cason Wallace could more than make up for the losses.

Of course, the two-time reigning MVP is still around too.

Even after last season's disappointing playoff exit, the Thunder have a real argument to start the season in the top spot in these rankings.

The San Antonio Spurs made the Finals ahead of schedule. Now, they have the opportunity to build on that success.

Victor Wembanyama, Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper are all still several years away from their primes. As scary as this prospect is, all three could (and probably should) be better than they were in 2025-26.

They beat the timeline a few months ago. Now, they look like perennial title contenders.

articles.title: 5 Trades That Should've Happened During 2026 NBA Offseason
articles.summary: NBA training camps are in full force, marking the official end of the 2026 offseason.
articles.body:
NBA training camps are in full force, marking the official end of the 2026 offseason.

There was no shortage of blockbuster trades, as players like Giannis Antetokounmpo, Jaylen Brown, Kawhi Leonard, Ja Morant, LaMelo Ball, Paul George, Brandon Ingram and others were all moved.

For all the big deals that transpired, it feels like a few more trades should have happened.

The San Antonio Spurs officially have a De'Aaron Fox problem with the emergence of Dylan Harper. The Golden State Warriors don't even look like a playoff team after a summer of inactivity. Kyrie Irving seems out of place on a rebuilding Dallas Mavericks squad.

Here are five trades that should (and still could!) have happened.

De'Aron Fox to Rockets, Dylan Harper Era Begins in San Antonio

The San Antonio Spurs didn't know they were going to have the opportunity to draft a guard like Dylan Harper when they originally traded for De'Aaron Fox. No one would blame them for wanting to move on from him now.

Fox was an All-Star last year and is still a really good player at age 28. Unfortunately for him, Harper and Stephon Castle are the backcourt of the future in San Antonio. Harper is way too good to play the sixth-man role for another season, as the Spurs had a net rating of plus-32.6 in the 700 possessions that Victor Wembanyama and Harper shared the floor without Fox. San Antonio needs to get their two stars on the court together as much as possible.

Fox going to the Houston Rockets makes a lot of sense, as Fred VanVleet is coming off a torn ACL at age 32 and head coach Ime Udoka didn't seem to trust Reed Sheppard just yet. Fox would be an upgrade over both, averaging 18.6 points, 3.8 rebounds, 6.2 assists and 1.2 steals per game last year.

A core of Fox, Amen Thompson, Kevin Durant, Tari Eason and Alperen Şengün could do some incredible damage, even in the West.

For the Spurs, a return of VanVleet and his expiring $25 million salary and Jabari Smith Jr. would be enough to make the money work. Fox is the best overall player in the deal, although San Antonio would get off of his four-year, $221 million contract and open up a starting job for Harper, which is the ultimate goal here.

Houston could ask for some draft compensation in return given the heftiness of Fox's contract, even if the two-time All-Star is a major upgrade over VanVleet.

The Milwaukee Bucks and Los Angeles Clippers likely won't rank high on your list of league pass teams, although both rosters could use some tweaking to maximize their season and watchability.

The center position for the Clippers is pretty rough right now. Brook Lopez is 38 years old and second-year big man Yanic Konan Niederhäuser underwent foot surgery in March to deal with a Lisfranc injury. With the Oklahoma City Thunder reserving the right to swap first-round picks with Los Angeles next summer, there's no incentive for the Clippers to lose. Upgrading the center spot is necessary.

Turner, 30, would bring his unique blend of three-point shooting (38.3 percent) and shot blocking (1.6 per game) to Los Angeles and should be widely available from a Milwaukee Bucks team that needs to create a bigger role for their own young center

Kel'el Ware is the best piece the Bucks received from the Miami Heat in the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade. Keeping him on the bench behind Turner would be a terrible mistake.

Ware, 22, is a true 7-footer who averaged 18.1 points, 14.0 rebounds and shot 51.4 percent from three in the 10 games in which he played at least 30 minutes last season. Milwaukee needs to make the former first-round pick a starter on Day 1.

The Bucks don't need a big return in exchange for Turner. The Clippers have some expiring contracts to send out if needed. This isn't the biggest trade, but it would improve both franchises now and in the future.

Kyrie Irving Brings His Magic to Orlando

Watching Kyrie Irving play basketball over the past 15 years has often been a magical experience. Few contenders need this kind of offensive boost more than the actual Magic.

Despite adding Desmond Bane last season to a core of Paolo Banchero, Franz Wagner and Jalen Suggs, Orlando ranked 18th in offense during the regular season and were dead last among the 16 playoff teams.

Constructing a deal that would send Suggs and picks, or other pieces, to the Dallas Mavericks in exchange for Irving makes too much sense for both teams.

The Magic are desperately trying to win now after three straight first-round playoff exits and could use Irving's ball-handling, playmaking, scoring and outside shooting to help transform the team's offense under new first-year head coach Sean Sweeney. Sweeney not only helped coach De'Aaron Fox to an All-Star season and develop Dylan Harper into a future star with the San Antonio Spurs last year, but he was also on the Mavericks' coaching staff with Irving from 2022 to 2025.

For Dallas, trading a 34-year-old Irving for a 25-year-old Suggs and other assets helps unite the timeline. Irving is coming off a torn ACL and may not be happy with the Mavs this season if they slip below the play-in tournament line.

The Mavs simply aren't ready to contend now around a 19-year-old Cooper Flagg. They need to do what's best for Flagg's next 10 years, not his next 10 months.

An Irving trade needs to happen at some point this season, with the Magic at the top of the list of teams who need him.

Ranking Every NBA Team's Starting Lineup Ahead of Preseason 🔢

Trey Murphy III, Dejounte Murray Keep Warriors In Title Hunt

The Golden State Warriors and New Orleans Pelicans had two of the NBA's worst offseasons after finishing 10th and 11th in the West last year, respectively.

It wasn't what the two franchises did, but rather what they didn't do.

Simply running back the vast majority of their cores won't be enough to make the Western Conference playoffs. Perhaps not even the play-in tournament, especially with the Utah Jazz and Dallas Mavericks looking much improved on paper.

As much as the Warriors would love to keep Jimmy Butler, waiting for the veteran forward to return from a torn ACL is going to doom the season. Kristaps Porziņģis and Moses Moody could both miss the start of the year as well.

Using Butler's expiring salary, along with a haul of first-round picks, to make a run at Trey Murphy III and Dejounte Murray could help save the Warriors' title hopes and benefit the Pelicans in the long run.

Murphy, 26, averaged 21.5 points, 5.7 rebounds, 3.8 assists, 1.5 steals and shot 37.9 percent from three last season. He'd immediately become the Warriors' starting small forward while Murray (16.7 points, 5.4 rebounds, 6.4 assists, 1.6 steals, plus-8.2 swing rating ) could start alongside Stephen Curry or become Golden State's sixth man.

For New Orleans, the move opens up a bigger role for second-year guard Jeremiah Fears and newly acquired wing Bennedict Mathurin. Butler could assist in a late-season playoff run or help open up cap space next summer when his $56.8 million salary comes off the books. The Pelicans should be asking for multiple first-round picks to complete such a deal, helping both franchises in the process.

Detroit Pistons Trade for Offensive-Minded Wing

The Detroit Pistons aren't going to sniff 60 wins again this season unless they can add a reliable No. 2 offensive option alongside Cade Cunningham. Simply swapping out Tobias Harris for John Collins does little to get this team closer to a championship.

The ideal trade target would be a wing who can create for themselves and others, helping to keep the offense humming when Cunningham needs a break or hits an inevitable shooting slump.

This list could include players like Tyler Herro, RJ Barrett, Lauri Markkanen, Franz Wagner or even Austin Reaves, should any become available.

Detroit has all of its first-round picks moving forward , making a potential blockbuster more likely. Former No. 5 overall pick Ron Holland II could be used as trade bait, as the runway hasn't been opened for him in Detroit to reach his potential.

The backbone of a great defense is already in place here and should be for years to come, with Ausar Thompson signing a five-year extension. Cunningham is arguably a top-10 player. There's a fair amount of shooting with Isaiah Joe added to the roster.

In the playoffs, however, this team becomes too predictable. Having a second guy who can create offense out of thin air is a must.

articles.title: Trade Ideas to Help Caitlin Clark, Fever After Early WNBA Playoff Loss
articles.summary: The Indiana Fever's 2026 season is officially over after a 94-83 loss to the Las Vegas Aces in Game 3 of the first round of the WNBA playoffs.
articles.body:
The Indiana Fever's 2026 season is officially over after a 94-83 loss to the Las Vegas Aces in Game 3 of the first round of the WNBA playoffs.

Let's be clear: Losing to prime A'ja Wilson in a winner-take-all game doesn't mean Indiana's season was a failure, especially when the Fever fought deep into the fourth quarter in their last loss. However, that doesn't mean there aren't clear areas where this roster needs to improve.

Indiana needs to get better defensively across the perimeter and add depth at center behind Aliyah Boston. However, the biggest question heading into the offseason is whether Kelsey Mitchell re-signs or goes elsewhere in free agency.

With that said, here are four trade ideas Indiana should consider this offseason, whether Mitchell returns or not.

Minnesota Lynx receive: Lexie Hull, 2027 first-round pick (No. 10), 2028 first-round pick

There might not be a team facing more uncertainty this offseason than Minnesota, with much of it hinging on Napheesa Collier's free agency decision. If Collier leaves, the Lynx could have to reconsider their timeline with their other three starters all entering their age-33 seasons or later, potentially opening the door for a retool around Olivia Miles.

Assuming Collier doesn't end up in Indiana (which, frankly, would be the dream scenario for the Fever), what if Indiana explored a trade for Kayla McBride, who is coming off an All-WNBA-caliber season?

McBride is the best movement shooter in the WNBA and an elite screener, making her an excellent fit alongside Caitlin Clark and Aliyah Boston. She's also an outstanding defender with great feel both on and off the ball. McBride would immediately become Indiana's best perimeter defender and address a major weakness for a defense that ranked last among all playoff teams.

The biggest obstacle is making the salary cap work. McBride has one year remaining on her contract and is set to make over $1.25 million in 2027. With Clark eligible for a max extension this offseason under the WNBA's EPIC provision—similar to the extension Boston signed last year—taking on McBride's salary would be difficult unless Kelsey Mitchell leaves in free agency.

Minnesota also has little reason to move McBride for a mediocre return, given how well she fits alongside Miles.

If Indiana isn't willing to trade two first-round picks, the Fever could send the No. 10 pick in the 2027 draft to Minnesota for the Lynx's No. 15 selection, along with Indiana's 2028 first-round pick. That would give Minnesota additional draft capital while allowing Indiana to move back just five spots in the first round.

New York Liberty receive: Lexie Hull, 2027 second-round pick (No. 10)

Would Satou Sabally help Indiana's defensive issues? Probably not. However, she has been linked to the Fever before, and with a salary of just $855,000, a trade could be feasible here.

A package centered around Lexie Hull and a second-round pick could make sense for both sides, especially given Sabally's injury history and Indiana's defensive concerns.

Sabally played just 13 games in 2026 after dealing with a knee cyst early in the season before suffering a severe concussion in late June that sidelined her for the remainder of the year. She has also missed more than 40 percent of her team's games since she was drafted in 2020.

If Sabally can stay healthy, imagine a lineup featuring Clark, Mitchell, Sabally and Boston.

New York, meanwhile, could use a 3-and-D wing like Hull. Rebecca Allen is retiring from the WNBA after this season and Rebekah Gardner is entering her age-37 season.

Indiana Fever receive: Monique Akoa-Makani, 2027 second-round pick (No. 16)

Los Angeles Sparks receive: Raven Johnson, 2027 first-round pick (No. 10)

There's no doubt Raven Johnson was a bright spot for Indiana against Las Vegas.

The 23-year-old averaged 7.3 points on 45 percent shooting from the field after stepping into the backup guard role for Ty Harris, who suffered a broken left fibula in the final game of the regular season.

But what if Indiana could acquire a more established player with a similar archetype to Johnson simply by moving back six spots in the 2027 draft? From the Fever's perspective, that would be an appealing tradeoff—though Los Angeles may require additional value to agree to it.

Monique Akoa-Makani wasn't quite as good in 2026 as she was in 2025, but she remains an elite point-of-attack defender. The 25-year-old is incredibly strong, has good size at 5'10" and has shot 39 percent from three over her first two seasons.

The question with Johnson is whether she'll ever become a good enough shooter to consistently space the floor next to Clark in the backcourt. Akoa-Makani is the better player right now, only a couple years older and would easily be the best perimeter defender on the roster.

Updated Playoff Bracket After Liberty Advance 😯

Indiana Fever receive: Olivia Nelson-Ododa

Houston Comets receive: Monique Billings, 2027 second-round pick, 2028 second-round pick

Indiana also needs to address its backup center spot. When Aliyah Boston was off the court this season, opponents shot 66.3 percent at the rim (a +7.9% swing), according to Databallr .

One option could be Olivia Nelson-Ododa, who averaged 10.1 points and 5.9 rebounds on 58.1 percent shooting from two for the Connecticut Sun this season. Those numbers jumped to 11.8 points and 7.3 rebounds when she started.

If Nelson-Ododa is your starting center, you probably aren't a particularly good team. But you feel pretty good if she's your backup behind Boston.

As Connecticut transitions to the Houston Comets next season, it could seek Monique Billings and a first-round pick in a deal. The Fever should prefer to limit their outgoing draft compensation to two second-rounders.

articles.title: Blazers Fire Broadcaster Braiden Bell After Past Racist, Sexist Social Media Posts Surface
articles.summary: A play-by-play broadcaster officially hired Thursday by the Portland Trail Blazers was dismissed the same day after previous racist and sexist posts were found on his social media account.
articles.body:
A play-by-play broadcaster officially hired Thursday by the Portland Trail Blazers was dismissed the same day after previous racist and sexist posts were found on his social media account.

The Trail Blazers announced the news in a statement stating the team has "zero tolerance for racist, sexist, or harmful comments."

The Trail Blazers announced earlier Thursday that Bell had been hired to call Blazers games alongside analyst Lamar Hurd.

Bell, 29, had previously called games for the Phoenix Mercury and the G League's Valley Suns.

The social media posts, first shared KGW's Devon Haskins, were published in 2012 and 2013, according to KGW .

KGW reached out to the Blazers for comment on Bell's old social media posts and received a response hours later stating Bell had been fired.

Bell was set to join a veteran team alongside Hurd, who has served in his role for the Blazers for 11 seasons alongside courtside reporter Brooke Olzendam, per KATU .

Veteran play-by-play broadcaster Kevin Calabro, who spent 22 years with the Seattle SuperSonics before joining the Trail Blazers in 2016, had his contract expire this summer, per The Athletic's Jason Quick .

Calabro told Quick he had decided not to return to the organization because he had received a contract offer he described as "not worth my time."

The Trail Blazers' sale to a group led by Tom Dundon, who also owns the Carolina Hurricanes, was approved by the NBA in March.

Dundon began his ownership of the Hurricanes in 2018 by firing the team's long-tenured radio broadcast team after Chuck Kaiton declined to take a significant pay cut, per Forbes' Maury Brown .

The Trail Blazers' new ownership group seemingly followed a similar playbook by dismissing multiple radio and television broadcasters.

The Blazers will now have to identify a new television play-by-play announcer with just five days to go until preseason and less than three weeks before the regular season begins Oct. 21 against the Phoenix Suns.

articles.title: Becky Hammon Drops Brutally Honest Quote After Being Asked About Fever, Aces 'Parallels'
articles.summary: Becky Hammon was dismissive of comparisons between her three-time champion Las Vegas Aces and the Indiana Fever after eliminating Caitlin Clark's team from the playoffs Thursday night.
articles.body:
Becky Hammon was dismissive of comparisons between her three-time champion Las Vegas Aces and the Indiana Fever after eliminating Caitlin Clark's team from the playoffs Thursday night.

When asked if she saw "parallels" between the Fever and the 2022 Aces, Hammon answered bluntly, "No."

Aces star A'ja Wilson laughed at the answer.

Harmon followed that up with, "I think that team has great potential, to answer your question. But it's different."

The Aces had never won a title before Hammon joined the team ahead of the 2022 campaign. A roster starring players including Wilson, Kelsey Plum, Jackie Young and Chelsea Gray went on to win the first of three championships in a span of four years that season.

The Fever, led by Clark alongside Aliyah Boston and Kelsey Mitchell, will be left still searching for their first title since 2012 following Friday night's 94-83 elimination loss to the Aces.

The Aces will now advance to face either the Golden State Valkyries or Dallas Wings in the 2026 WNBA semifinals.

articles.title: Victor Wembanyama said no to gambling money. In today’s NBA, that feels radical
articles.summary: As LeBron James and other NBA stars wholeheartedly embrace the murk of betting and prediction markets, the San Antonio Spurs’ 22-year-old cornerstone has dra...
articles.body:
If the song from LeBron James's agonizing Polymarket ad is as stuck in your head as mine thanks to the commercial playing during every YouTube video and HBO show (all I wanted to do was rewatch The Leftovers), let Victor Wembanyama be your antidote. At the Spurs' practice on Thursday, San Antonio Express-News columnist Mike Finger asked Wembanyama if he would ever partner with a sports betting firm. It couldn't have been easier for the 22-year-old to say yes. The NBA displays ads for both FanDuel and DraftKings, in addition to hawking betting odds on its broadcasts. Until the streaming service met its end a few months ago, plenty of NBA games streamed exclusively on FanDuel Sports Network. Then there are Wembanyama's legendary peers: James is the new face of Polymarket; Kevin Durant reads FanDuel odds and invests in Kalshi; Giannis Antetokounmpo is a Kalshi shareholder.

"Absolutely not," Wembanyama said instead . "I will never do that. Honestly, I think it's very sad to see some players promote it. Everybody does whatever they want, but without me."

Standards are so back. It shouldn't feel miraculous that a star of Wembanyama's stature is taking the position that players should not cash checks from predatory companies that incentivize athletes to dabble in insider trading, but in 2026, we'll take any anti-sellout ally we can find. This one may prove particularly valuable. Given his age and fame, Wembanyama should be around as a beacon to cut through the murk of betting for some time to come. How refreshing that, as rightwing terror reigns, the NBA's best and biggest young star is a politically outspoken leftist.

It's not a stylish time to turn down buckets of money. Thanks to some combination of a disintegrating economy, a president and political party so craven and corrupt that scandal-worthy behavior often doesn't register, and a significant overlap among the wealthy and the morally bankrupt, shame died a bloody death somewhere in the last decade. Most basketball podcasts keep themselves afloat with gambling companies' life rings. No reputational damage seems to last. James's Polymarket partnership was immediately and emphatically unpopular, but apparently not enough for anybody at the Philadelphia 76ers' media day to ask him about it.

So Wembanyama's emphatic rejection of a sports betting partnership stands out. Had he simply said, "Sure, who knows what the future brings," few would have batted an eye. But not only did he refuse the possibility, he also left behind a receipt. I will never do that. For Wembanyama, any eventual embrace of gambling will be met with fans' usual criticism – and his own words echoed back at him.

What's perhaps most refreshing about Wembanyama is – so far, at least; athletes tend to become more and more PR-friendly as they age – his willingness to ruffle feathers. Asked about the murders of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by ICE agents in January, Wembanyama said, "Yeah, PR has tried, but I'm not going to sit here and give some politically correct [answer]. Every day I wake up and see the news, and I'm horrified. I think it's crazy that some people might make it seem like or sound like the murder of civilians is acceptable." It's similarly outrageous that the aggressive integration of sports betting and prediction markets into society has been successful. It's not normal or ideal for professional sports leagues to be in bed with gambling firms, or for companies that allow people to trade money on every event imaginable to exist at all. A healthy NBA is one where the star poised to dominate the league for the next decade is willing to express sentiment along those lines out loud.

There is one cynical way to look at Wembanyama's response. He's coming off a run of bad press on the court. After a brilliant playoff run through three rounds, he had a disastrous NBA finals. He threw a pass off a teammate's back in the decisive moments of one game, missed two free throws towards the end of another (in which the Spurs failed to consolidate a 29-point lead into victory). He showed flashes of violence in the playoffs, earning an ejection by elbowing Naz Reid in the neck, and at times succumbed to the same brand of foul-baiting he'd criticized in other players months earlier. As the Spurs crashed out, Wemby had never been less popular. Decrying the omnipresence of sports betting, which fans almost universally abhor, gets the Spurs' big man back in their good graces. But it's hard to say his swing in fortune is undeserved. Fun as it is to watch, what happens during a professional basketball game is rarely more than a metaphor for society. A clear appraisal of the real world is more representative of virtue.

articles.title: A’ja Wilson Pulls Off WNBA Playoff Feat Nobody Has Done Before
articles.summary: A’ja Wilson entered Thursday night with the Las Vegas Aces facing elimination. A loss to Indiana would end their title defense, while a win would send them t...
articles.body:
A'ja Wilson entered Thursday night with the Las Vegas Aces facing elimination. A loss to Indiana would end their title defense, while a win would send them to the next round.

Wilson had already delivered in many big playoff games. She also led the WNBA with 26.2 points per game during the 2026 regular season before Indiana forced a deciding Game 3.

A'ja Wilson Delivers With The Season On The Line

Wilson scored 36 points, grabbed 10 rebounds and blocked two shots as Las Vegas beat Indiana 94-83. The win sent the Aces to the semifinals for the eighth straight season.

According to playoff tracking cited after the game, Wilson became the first WNBA player to score at least 30 points in three straight elimination games. She also reached 12 career playoff games with at least 30 points, another league record.

Wilson opened the series with 38 points and 16 rebounds while making 15 of 19 shots. Indiana responded by holding her to 22 points in Game 2 and winning 99-89 to force a deciding game.

Wilson made 11 of 18 shots in Game 3 to lead Las Vegas. Chelsea Gray added 23 points, while Jackie Young finished with 18 points, eight rebounds and seven assists.

The Numbers Behind A'ja Wilson's Playoff Performance

Wilson averaged 32 points in the series and made 62.5% of her shots. Those numbers show how consistently she scored despite Indiana's defensive pressure.

The cited tracking figures said defenders challenged 39 of her 48 shots, or about 81% of her attempts. They also listed a 79% success rate on those contested shots, but that figure conflicts with her overall shooting percentage.

Indiana still threatened to end Las Vegas' season late in Game 3. The Fever cut the lead to two with three minutes remaining, but the Aces held on behind Wilson's 36 points and 10 rebounds.

Wilson's career already includes four WNBA MVP awards, three championships and three Finals MVP awards. She also led the league in scoring for the third time this season.

Her latest record adds another first to that career. No other WNBA player has scored at least 30 points in three straight playoff games when a loss would have ended their team's season.
