articles.title: Veronica Burton went from overlooked to indispensable with the Golden State Valkyries
articles.summary: OAKLAND, Calif. — In the historic Australian gold rush town of Bendigo, Veronica Burton felt great but had no idea how good it would get. Her WNBA career had...
articles.body:
OAKLAND, Calif. — In the historic Australian gold rush town of Bendigo, Veronica Burton felt great but had no idea how good it would get.

Her WNBA career had been a wisp. Three seasons. Not much court time or production.

Playing the best basketball of her professional career, even overseas, colored the picture Burton had of herself. It also didn't guarantee anyone back home would see her that way.

In fact, the Connecticut Sun had already informed Burton she'd be unprotected in the forthcoming expansion draft. Feeling unwanted isn't fun. Feeling like you're floating in space is something else. Who knew if this new franchise in the Bay Area would select her. Who knew if she'd have to return to a club with minimal belief in her. Who knew if this WNBA pursuit would leave her with little more than a handful of pyrite crystals.

"It was almost like a make-or-break in a sense," Burton said. "I knew I could carve out a role in this league, but I could have gone either way for sure."

She's sitting in a lobby down the hall from the Golden State Valkyries' practice gym, on an off-day amid a pursuit of a championship, which spoils the ending but not the moral.

The roster math of an expansion era has created more opportunity in one of the hardest leagues in the world to make. No player benefitted more, or took better advantage, than a 5-foot-9 guard who has become one of the WNBA's most valuable assets because she got the chance to.

It required Burton to loosen her grip while running a high-functioning operation, and it required a coach willing to help a fastidious point guard navigate that paradox. And when the 2026 regular season ended, four-time MVP A'ja Wilson of the Las Vegas Aces sat atop the leaderboard for win shares, a measure of a single player's contribution to team success. In second place? Burton, who averaged 2.6 points before she got here.

"When you get poured into, when you get treated like a professional, when people and your teammates believe in you, then you can see the difference," 14-year veteran Tiffany Hayes said of Burton. "Her standing and believing in herself, not giving it up, it's a testament to her and who she is. And that's why she's our leader."

Ever-excitable Warriors and Valkyries co-owner Joe Lacob predicted a title within five years for an upstart franchise already valued at a billion dollars . Still, he couldn't have known it could happen sooner because the front office scooped a franchise point guard off the discard pile.

A breakout arrived immediately, when both the Valkyries — and, arguably, Burton herself — existed in a real way for the first time.

She played almost as much in Year 1 with Golden State (1,292 minutes) as she had in three seasons with Dallas and Connecticut combined (1,496). She won the league's Most Improved Player award, made second-team All-Defense and finished ninth in MVP balloting. Her numbers this season, in every meaningful category, were the same or better.

In summary, Burton stopped being afraid of what might happen when she tried to make things happen. Her club is now one win away from the semifinals, entering Friday night's Game 3 against the Dallas Wings.

"I've come into myself and been surrounded by people that fully see me, what I bring to the table," she said. "I think that allows me to play with that freedom rather than a timidness. When I play timid basketball, I'm not a very good basketball player, and it doesn't go well for me."

When she entered the WNBA in 2022 after an All-Big Ten career at Northwestern, 144 spots were available across 12 teams. Those are suffocating odds, even for a player selected seventh in the draft. After all, two years after Dallas selected Burton in the first round, it waived her before the season began.

In this context, Burton's control-freak tendencies — "I like everything to go exactly how I planned it or envisioned it, and that's just not reality," she said now — were more of a liability than a strength.

During training camps, every play felt like a final exam. If it was OK to make a mistake, she didn't know it, and no one convinced her otherwise.

"I just had this hyper-awareness of every single thing that I was doing to a fault," Burton said.

The situation in Golden State, in a way, exerted even more pressure. If Burton couldn't establish herself with an expansion franchise, what then?

In this, the clever mind tricks of her new coach, Natalie Nakase, were a release. Nakase asks every player how she wants to be coached, and then she coaches them that way. Some want to be yelled at. Some want to be pulled aside for corrections instead of public flogging.

When asked, Burton said she thrives with a coach who believes in her.

"Every shot, anything we did," Nakase said, "positive reinforcement, positive reinforcement."

Burton's very first line for Golden State put the theory to the test. A little more than 17 minutes played, with zero field goals and only three assists in a blowout loss to the Los Angeles Sparks.

She might've sensed unsettled ground below her feet as she began the obligatory film breakdown with Nakase. However, her mistakes weren't crimes. From her new coach's perspective, they were necessary.

"She's just like, 'I don't care if you turn the ball over,'" Burton recalled. "'You're not trying to turn the ball over. I get what you're seeing here.' And I think that was, again, a level of reassurance that I hadn't had."

Relinquishing a desire to control every outcome was a big deal. It doesn't happen, though, without permission.

"I didn't feel like I had to continue to prove myself every single day," Burton said.

Now she's an emblem, among a growing collection of them.

Marina Mabrey matriculated to the expansion Toronto Tempo, improved her per-100-possession scoring by 12 points and made her first All-Star team in 2026. With the first-year Portland Fire, guard Carla Leite doubled her scoring (7.2 points to 16.1 points) and tripled her assist output (2.0 to 6.3) after Golden State left her unprotected. Veteran center Megan DiLeo never averaged more than 7.9 points or started more than seven games in her first seven WNBA seasons. She averaged 13.1 points and started 32 games for the Fire this year.

Stars spotted for the first time, when maybe you couldn't find them with a telescope before. With three more teams on the way before 2030 — in Cleveland , Detroit and Philadelphia — the sky gets even wider.

Still, Burton remembers the dark. Or maybe it's more like she can't forget it. It's why she immediately contacted Golden State fan favorite Kate Martin when Martin was let go near the end of training camp, and why she welcomed Martin over for a taco dinner with former Valkyries teammates when Martin and her new team, the Sparks, came through San Francisco for the first time this summer.

"Whenever anyone gets cut in this league, it's brutal," Burton said. "You build all these relationships and then suddenly your life just kind of shifts. So any roster change that happens, I try to reach out and remind people that this isn't the end of their story or the end of their career. And, honestly, it could be just a new beginning for them."

Sometimes, it's stunning what you unearth when you dig into new ground.

"I didn't even know the Golden State Valkyries were going to be a thing," Burton said, "and here I am."

articles.title: Bub Carrington Says 'It's No Secret' Wizards Were 'Held Back' to Land AJ Dybantsa in 2026 NBA Draft
articles.summary: Washington Wizards guard Bub Carrington came out and said what most were probably already thinking Thursday regarding the organization's pursuit of the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NBA draft.
articles.body:
Washington Wizards guard Bub Carrington came out and said what most were probably already thinking Thursday regarding the organization's pursuit of the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NBA draft.

During an interview with WUSA9 (beginning at the 27:20 mark of the video) , Carrington said, "We just haven't been told yet to go be the best version of yourself. We've all, in a way, been held back just because we were trying to get AJ Dybantsa. That's no secret. But now, no one has handcuffs. Everyone is shackles-free."

Ranking Every NBA Team's Starting Lineup Ahead of Preseason 🔢

According to The Athletic's Sam Amick and Josh Robbins , "the NBA is not expected to discipline Carrington or the Wizards for his comments."

Washington went just 17-65 last season, marking the third consecutive year it won 20 or fewer games. On that occasion, though, it was lucky enough to win the NBA draft lottery, which allowed the Wiz to select BYU forward AJ Dybantsa first overall.

The NBA's new lottery system for 2027 was created in large part to curtail intentional losing or "tanking," and Carrington's comments suggest that was a very real issue the league was facing before the new rules were implemented.

articles.title: Everything Caitlin Clark Said About Ref Calls, WNBA Offseason After Fever's Playoff Elimination
articles.summary: Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark appeared unhappy to see her team finish Thursday night's elimination loss to the Las Vegas Aces having been called for eight more fouls than the defending champions.
articles.body:
Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark appeared unhappy to see her team finish Thursday night's elimination loss to the Las Vegas Aces having been called for eight more fouls than the defending champions.

The Fever were called for 27 fouls, while the Aces were flagged 19 times in their 94-83 win in Game 3 of the first round.

Fever coach Stephanie White pointed out after the elimination loss the Aces had taken 35 free throws to the Fever's 20.

The Aces closed out the win having gone 28-for-35 from the foul line, while the Fever made 14 of their 20 attempts.

Clark was visibly frustrated with officials late in the game after no foul was called on a play during which an inadvertent elbow from the Aces' Jewell Loyd left her with a bloodied mouth.

Clark said she planned to turn her attention to getting some rest this offseason after a busy year following her return from the injuries that limited her during her sophomore WNBA campaign.

"I didn't take a break when our season ended last year. So, I've been going for almost, what, a year and a half... I haven't taken a break from the game in a really long time," Clark said Thursday night. "It's been a long grind, but a really fun one, and a very rewarding one."

Clark continued, "I didn't play much last year, but I was able to come out here and put together the best season I've had, and perform at a really high level, and basically get better in every area.

"Still feel like I have so many areas to improve, so I guess that's the most exciting part moving forward. You know I love the work. I love being in the gym. So I'll probably be kicked out for a little white, but we'll get back to it."

This marks the second straight season in which the Fever, who went to the semifinals last season without an injured Clark, have been eliminated by the Aces.

The Aces will now begin preparing for a semifinal matchup against the Golden State Valkyries or Dallas Wings.

articles.title: New Lakers Rumors on Dalton Knecht's Future, 'Odd Man Out' on Roster Ahead of NBA Season
articles.summary: Dalton Knecht's career with the Los Angeles Lakers could potentially be over just two years after the franchise selected him in the first round of the 2024 draft.
articles.body:
Dalton Knecht's career with the Los Angeles Lakers could potentially be over just two years after the franchise selected him in the first round of the 2024 draft.

The California Post 's Khobi Price reported Friday "multiple rival executives expect" Knecht "to be the odd man out as the Lakers look to trim their roster from 16 players on standard NBA deals to the league maximum of 15."

ClutchPoints' Brett Siegel reported last week he expected "a lot of pressure on Dalton Knecht to fight for this roster spot with Jaden Hardy in training camp" (h/t ClutchPoints' Julian Ojeda ).

Biggest Training Camp Questions for the Lakers 🤔

Lakers coach JJ Redick recently named Hardy as a player he thought would be able to take on some ball-handling duties when Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves aren't running the offense "if he's in the lineup" this season (h/t Lakers Nation's Daniel Starkand).

When asked about Knecht on Thursday, Redick said he had enjoyed a "good three days of practice" and was "hungry to earn a spot in the rotation."

The Lakers acquired Hardy alongside two second-round picks this July as part of the Deandre Ayton trade. He averaged 9.2 points in 15.8 minutes per game last season in a campaign split between the Washington Wizards and Dallas Mavericks.

Knecht, selected by the Lakers 17th overall in the 2024 draft, appeared in 78 games of his rookie season while contributing 9.1 points in 19.2 minutes per game.

He fell out of Redick's regular rotation in his sophomore NBA campaign, at times struggling on defense while averaging 4.2 points in a 10.2 minutes per game through 54 contests.

Knecht went through a midseason shooting slump, shooting 22.2 percent from deep in 12 games in January before slipping out of the rotation entirely down the stretch.

The third-year wing said earlier this week he hopes his shooting, rebounding and more "high effort on the defensive end" will keep him in the Lakers lineup.

Whether Knecht is able to show that development in the preseason, starting next Monday at the Sacramento Kings, could be key to whether he remains in the Lakers' plans by the time Opening Day rosters are due Oct. 19 at 5 p.m. ET.

articles.title: After another early exit, Caitlin Clark’s career is still lacking playoff success
articles.summary: As undeniable as Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark is as a WNBA megastar, both in terms of her on-court prowess and off-court attention, it is also undeniable that Clark is missing what is often considered the hallmark of true greatness for any basketball player: playoff heroics.
articles.body: As undeniable as Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark is as a WNBA megastar, both in terms of her on-court prowess and off-court attention, it is also undeniable that Clark is missing what is often considered the hallmark of true greatness for any basketball player: playoff heroics. Clark and the Fever were eliminated from the postseason Thursday, losing 94-83 to the Las Vegas Aces in a winner-take-all Game 3 to cap their first-round series. And Clark put up a dispiriting performance, finishing with only 18 points and four assists. She was inefficient, hitting only 6 of 18 field goals (including a bricky 3 of 12 from 3) while committing six turnovers. Clark’s play paled in comparison to four-time MVP A’ja Wilson, who had 36 points and 10 rebounds on 61.1% shooting. “Obviously, probably let this hurt a little bit,” Clark said after the game when asked to look back on the Fever’s season and exit. “This is really only my fifth game playing in the postseason, so you kind of take the burn a little bit, but also how much fun this season was and how together our group was and just getting to replicate that going forward.” As Clark mentioned, her relative playoff inexperience is somewhat surprising for a player of her caliber. She played in only two postseason games in her rookie season, in which the Fever were swept in the first round by the Connecticut Sun. Last year, Clark missed the playoffs entirely due to a groin injury and bone bruise in her left ankle. Clark was healthy this season and had her best year as a pro. She finished third in scoring with 22.3 points per game and was the only player in the WNBA to average at least 22 points and eight assists a night. That made Clark’s playoff performance even more disappointing, as her scoring and efficiency dipped, while her turnovers increased. Clark especially struggled in Indiana’s two losses, averaging only 16.5 points with 7.0 assists and 6.0 turnovers across those games. For the entire series, Clark shot 39.6% from the field and 33.3% from deep. “We’ve got to give credit to the Aces,” Clark said. “I thought they played well. I thought they were ready to go. That’s what championship teams do.” She added: “They made it difficult, but we’ve made a lot of those shots throughout the year, too. At the same time, we were right there despite some of the poor shooting.” There are legitimate reasons why Clark has not enjoyed the same level of playoff success as some of the game’s other established stars: Clark is still in the early stages of her career, she lost most of her second season to injury, the Fever were a struggling franchise when she was drafted, the three-game first round is a small sample size, and the competition in the W has never been better. Several of the game’s legends, from OGs such as Lisa Leslie and Candace Parker to current greats such as Wilson, didn’t race out of the gate winning championships early in their careers. But Thursday was likely the biggest game of Clark’s professional career so far. Her play and her team’s loss proved she is still searching for the kind of accomplishments that will ultimately come to define her career. “I was able to come out here and put together the best season I’ve had and perform at a really high level and basically get better in every area and still feel like I have so many areas to improve,” Clark said. “So, I guess that’s the most exciting part moving forward. I love the work. I love being in the gym. So, I’ll probably be kicked out for a little while, but we’ll get back to it.”

articles.title: NBA 2026-27 Key Dates for All-Star Weekend Schedule, Trade Deadline and More
articles.summary: October has arrived and with it will soon come the opening tip of the 2026-27 NBA season.
articles.body:
October has arrived and with it will soon come the opening tip of the 2026-27 NBA season.

From there, an 82-game marathon will stretch across six more months, featuring an in-season tournament, some loaded holiday slates, a perhaps hyper active trade deadline and the annual celebration of the Association known as All-Star Weekend.

It should be a thrill ride from start to finish, and you'll surely want to catch as much of it as possible. To help you do just that, we'll provide all the need-to-know dates to put on your calender before digging into a couple of the biggest stories stemming from the recently opened training camps.

Oct. 30: Emirates NBA Cup Group Play tips off

Nov. 27: Emirates NBA Cup Group Play concludes

Dec. 4-5: Emirates NBA Cup Quarterfinals

Dec. 8 and/or Dec. 9: Emirates NBA Cup Semifinals

Jan. 10: All NBA contracts are guaranteed for the remainder of the season

Camp Buzz: Pistons Finally Sign Jalen Duren

It may have taken forever and a day for pen to reach paper, but the Detroit Pistons and Jalen Duren finally ended his extended stay in restricted free agency. Both sides came together on a fully guaranteed five-year, $200 million deal, as ESPN's Shams Charania first reported.

Duren's free agency always figured to be tricky, but few could've foreseen the stalemate sticking this long. He was difficult to price, though, since his breakout 2025-26 season (featuring his first All-Star and All-NBA selections) was immediately followed by a shaky playoff showing.

While the two are officially reunited, time only knows what (if any) damage was done to this relationship along the way. Per Charania , Duren's "representatives made it clear that he felt disrespected by the process" and "took issue with weight clasues in some of the team's previous offers."

Maybe the often ugly business side of basketball gets left at the negotiating table, and everyone can move on as if this never happened. But this situation will be highly scrutinized, especially if Duren and/or Detroit struggle to build off of their 2025-26 regular-season success.

Camp Buzz: Point-LeBron Running Philly Offense?

The Philadelphia 76ers will arguably carry the most loaded-on-paper lineup into the new campaign. They'll also have a ton of mouths to feed within an offense now featuring two former MVPs (LeBron James and Joel Embiid) and two 2025-26 All-NBA honorees (Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown).

While the Sixers will need to collectively manage their egos and play their respective parts offensively, they'll also probably need someone to get this offense organized. It sounds like that someone will be the 41-year-old James more often than not:

James has only spent five percent of his career point guards as a nominal point guard, per Basketball-Reference, but he knows this role as well as anyone. Most of his offensive ecosystems have orbited around him, and he has dished out the fourth-most career assists in NBA history (12,016 and counting).

If James has a signature skill beyond his unprecedented longevity, it's probably his cerebral approach to the game. It makes sense, then, for the Sixers to lean into that intelligence and task him with getting all of the puzzle pieces properly sorted.
